dmm-2022-power-01a.title: Compute
dmm-2022-power-01a.body: Xavier's ranks are $1$ (Alice), $2$ (Bob), $2$ (Cady): $\frac{1+2+2}3=\frac53$. Yisa's ranks are $2,3,1$: $\frac{2+3+1}3=2$. Zack's score is $\frac73$. Since $\frac53<2<\frac73$, Xavier has the smallest Borda score and wins. ∎

dmm-2022-power-01b.title: Example
dmm-2022-power-01b.body: Yes. Let the fourth voter rank Yisa $>$ Zack $>$ Xavier. The Borda scores become: Xavier $\frac{1+2+2+3}4=2$, Yisa $\frac{2+3+1+1}4=\frac74$, Zack $\frac{3+1+3+2}4=\frac94$. Yisa has the smallest score and wins. ∎

dmm-2022-power-02a.title: Counterexample
dmm-2022-power-02a.body: No. Take the election with five voters and four candidates: $v_1,v_2,v_3$: $c_1>c_2>c_3>c_4$; $v_4,v_5$: $c_4>c_2>c_3>c_1$. Then $c_1$ is ranked first by $3$ of $5$ voters, but the Borda scores are $c_1:\frac{1+1+1+4+4}5=\frac{11}5$, $c_2:2$, $c_3:3$, $c_4:\frac{4+4+4+1+1}5=\frac{14}5$. So $c_2$ wins, not $c_1$. ∎

dmm-2022-power-02b.title: Scores move the right way
dmm-2022-power-02b.body: Yes. Improving $c$'s position in a vote strictly decreases $r_v(c)$, so the Borda score of $c$ decreases. Every other candidate's rank in that vote either stays the same or increases by $1$ (a candidate passed by $c$ moves down one place), so their Borda scores do not decrease. Hence $c$ still has the smallest Borda score. ∎

dmm-2022-power-02c.title: Counterexample
dmm-2022-power-02c.body: No. Use the election from 2(a): $v_1,v_2,v_3$: $c_1>c_2>c_3>c_4$; $v_4,v_5$: $c_4>c_2>c_3>c_1$, where $c_2$ wins with Borda score $2$. Change the votes of $v_4$ and $v_5$ to $c_4>c_2>c_1>c_3$. Candidates ranked below $c_2$ in a vote of $v_4,v_5$ were $c_3,c_1$, and they are still below $c_2$; the other votes are unchanged. Now the scores are $c_1:\frac{1+1+1+3+3}5=\frac95$, $c_2:2$, $c_3:\frac{3+3+3+4+4}5=\frac{17}5$, $c_4:\frac{14}5$. So $c_1$ wins and $c_2$ no longer does. ∎

dmm-2022-power-03a.title: Check all committees
dmm-2022-power-03a.body: The committee $\{c_2,c_4\}$ gives best ranks $2,1,2,2,1$ for $v_1,\dots,v_5$ (ranks of $c_2$: $2,1,2,3,3$ and of $c_4$: $4,3,5,2,1$), so its score is $\frac{2+1+2+2+1}5=\frac85$. Checking all $\binom52=10$ committees, every other committee has a larger score: the next best are $\{c_1,c_2\}$ and $\{c_1,c_3\}$ with score $\frac95$. So the answer is $\{c_2,c_4\}$ with score $\frac85$.

dmm-2022-power-03b.title: Counterexample
dmm-2022-power-03b.body: No. Use the election of 2(a): $v_1,v_2,v_3:c_1>c_2>c_3>c_4$; $v_4,v_5:c_4>c_2>c_3>c_1$. The single candidates have scores $c_1:\frac{11}5$, $c_2:2$, $c_3:3$, $c_4:\frac{14}5$, so $T_1^*=\{c_2\}$. The committee $\{c_1,c_4\}$ has score $1$ (every voter has $c_1$ or $c_4$ in first place), which is the minimum possible, and a score of $1$ requires the committee to contain both first choices $c_1$ and $c_4$. So $T_2^*=\{c_1,c_4\}\not\supset\{c_2\}=T_1^*$. ∎

dmm-2022-power-03c.title: Expected minimum of a random subset
dmm-2022-power-03c.body:
By linearity of expectation it suffices to compute the expected best rank for one voter $v$. Since $T$ is a uniformly random $k$-subset of the candidates, the set of ranks $\{r_v(c):c\in T\}$ is a uniformly random $k$-subset $K$ of $\{1,\dots,m\}$, and $r_v(T)=\min K$. For $t\ge1$, $P(\min K\ge t)=\binom{m-t+1}k/\binom mk$, so
$$\mathbf E[\min K]=\sum_{t=1}^mP(\min K\ge t)=\frac{1}{\binom mk}\sum_{t=1}^m\binom{m-t+1}{k}=\frac{\binom{m+1}{k+1}}{\binom mk}=\frac{m+1}{k+1},$$
using the hockey-stick identity $\sum_{j=1}^m\binom jk=\binom{m+1}{k+1}$. This is the same for every voter, so the average over voters is $\frac{m+1}{k+1}$, independent of $n$. ∎

dmm-2022-power-03c.title: Gaps on a circle
dmm-2022-power-03c.body: Put $m+1$ points on a circle (the $m$ ranks and one extra point $0$) and choose a uniformly random set of $k+1$ of them, then a uniformly random one $P$ of these $k+1$ points as origin. After rotating so $P=0$, the other $k$ points form a uniformly random $k$-subset of $\{1,\dots,m\}$. The $k+1$ gaps between consecutive chosen points sum to $m+1$, and since the origin is a uniformly random chosen point, all gaps have the same expectation, $\frac{m+1}{k+1}$. The smallest rank in the subset is the first gap from the origin, so $\mathbf E[\min K]=\frac{m+1}{k+1}$. ∎

dmm-2022-power-04a.title: Run Greedy
dmm-2022-power-04a.body: Round $1$: the single-candidate scores are $c_2:\frac{11}5$ (smallest), $c_1:\frac{13}5$, $c_4:3$, ... so $c_2$ is chosen. Round $2$: adding $c_4$ gives $\frac85$, the smallest ($c_1$ and $c_3$ give $\frac95$). Round $3$: adding any of $c_1,c_3,c_5$ gives the same Borda score $\frac75$ (and $c_1$ is one of the tied best choices). With $c_1$ chosen, Greedy produces $\{c_1,c_2,c_4\}$. ∎

dmm-2022-power-04b.title: Counterexample
dmm-2022-power-04b.body: No. Take the election of 2(a): $v_1,v_2,v_3:c_1>c_2>c_3>c_4$; $v_4,v_5:c_4>c_2>c_3>c_1$. The best committee of size $2$ is $\{c_1,c_4\}$ with score $1$. Greedy first picks $c_2$ (score $2$, the smallest single score), and then adding $c_1$ gives $\frac{1+1+1+2+2}5=\frac75$, adding $c_4$ gives $\frac{2+2+2+1+1}5=\frac85$, adding $c_3$ gives $2$. So Greedy produces $\{c_1,c_2\}$ with score $\frac75>1$. ∎

dmm-2022-power-04c.body:
For $c

For a voter $v$ with $ho=r_v(T_j)$, adding $c$ improves $v$'s best rank by $ho-r_v(c)$ if $r_v(c)<ho$ and by $0$ otherwise. dmm-2022-power-05a.title: Induction using 4(c) and Cauchy-Schwarz
dmm-2022-power-05a.body:
Write $\bar r_j=r_{\mathcal V}(T_j)$. We prove $\bar r_k\le\frac{2(m+1)}{k+1}$ by induction on $k$.

**Base case $k=1$.** Greedy picks the candidate of smallest Borda score, which is at most the average Borda score $\frac{m+1}2$, so $\bar r_1\le\frac{m+1}2\le m+1$.

**Step.** Let $k\ge2$ and assume $\bar r_{k-1}\le\frac{2(m+1)}k$. If $\bar r_{k-1}\le\frac{2(m+1)}{k+1}$ we are done since scores do not increase ($\bar r_k\le\bar r_{k-1}$). So assume
$$\frac{2(m+1)}{k+1}<\bar r_{k-1}\le\frac{2(m+1)}{k}.$$
Let $\rho_v=r_v(T_{k-1})$, so $\sum_v\rho_v=n\bar r_{k-1}$. By Cauchy-Schwarz $\sum_v\rho_v^2\ge\frac1n\left(\sum_v\rho_v\right)^2=n\bar r_{k-1}^2$. By 4(c) with $j=k-1$,
$$\bar r_{k-1}-\bar r_k\ge\frac{\sum_v\rho_v^2-\sum_v\rho_v}{2n(m-k+1)}\ge\frac{n\bar r_{k-1}^2-n\bar r_{k-1}}{2n(m-k+1)}=\frac{\bar r_{k-1}^2}{2(m-k+1)}\left(1-\frac1{\bar r_{k-1}}\right).$$
Since $\bar r_{k-1}>\frac{2(m+1)}{k+1}$, we have $1-\frac1{\bar r_{k-1}}>1-\frac{k+1}{2(m+1)}=\frac{2m+1-k}{2(m+1)}$, so
$$\bar r_{k-1}-\bar r_k\ge\bar r_{k-1}^2\cdot\frac{2m+1-k}{4(m+1)(m-k+1)}\ge\frac{\bar r_{k-1}^2}{2(m+1)},$$
because $\frac{2m+1-k}{2(m-k+1)}\ge1\iff k\ge1$. Therefore
$$\bar r_k\le f(\bar r_{k-1}),\qquad f(t)=t-\frac{t^2}{2(m+1)}.$$
The function $f$ is increasing for $t\le m+1$, and $\bar r_{k-1}\le\frac{2(m+1)}k\le m+1$, so
$$\bar r_k\le f\!\left(\frac{2(m+1)}k\right)=\frac{2(m+1)}k-\frac{2(m+1)}{k^2}=\frac{2(m+1)(k-1)}{k^2}\le\frac{2(m+1)}{k+1},$$
since $(k-1)(k+1)\le k^2$. This completes the induction, and $\frac{2(m+1)}{k+1}=2\,\mathrm{Rand}(k)$. ∎

dmm-2022-power-05b.title: A construction
dmm-2022-power-05b.body:
Take an even $m\ge6$, $k=2$, and $n=(m-1)!$ voters: candidate $c_1$ is ranked in position $\frac m2$ by every voter, and the other $m-1$ candidates fill the remaining positions in every possible order (each of the $(m-1)!$ orders appears exactly once).

**Round 1.** For $c\ne c_1$ the position of $c$ among the $m-1$ other candidates is uniform in $\{1,\dots,m-1\}$ and its true rank is $\rho$ if $\rho<\frac m2$ and $\rho+1$ otherwise. Its average rank is
$$\frac{1}{m-1}\left[\sum_{\rho=1}^{m/2-1}\rho+\sum_{\rho=m/2}^{m-1}(\rho+1)\right]=\frac{m^2}{2(m-1)}>\frac m2,$$
which is larger than $c_1$'s score $\frac m2$. So Greedy picks $c_1$.

**Round 2.** Adding any $c\ne c_1$ (all equivalent by symmetry) gives the average of $\min(\frac m2,\mathrm{rank}(c))$, which equals
$$\frac1{m-1}\left[\sum_{\rho=1}^{m/2-1}\rho+\frac m2\cdot\frac m2\right]=\frac{m(3m-2)}{8(m-1)}.$$
So $r_{\mathcal V}(T_2)=\frac{m(3m-2)}{8(m-1)}$, while $\mathrm{Rand}(2)=\frac{m+1}3$. We have $\frac{m(3m-2)}{8(m-1)}>\frac{m+1}3\iff9m^2-6m>8m^2-8\iff(m-2)(m-4)>0$, true for $m\ge6$. For example $m=6$ (with $n=120$ voters): $\frac{12}5=2.4>\frac73\approx2.33$. ∎

dmm-2022-power-06a.title: Plain English
dmm-2022-power-06a.body: For each voter, look at the $s$ members of the committee that this voter ranks highest (smallest ranks) and add up their ranks; this is the minimum over all $s$-element subsets $Q$ of the committee. The $s$-Borda score is the average of this number over all voters. (For $s=1$ it is the ordinary committee Borda score.)

dmm-2022-power-06b.title: Compare all committees
dmm-2022-power-06b.body: For $T=\{c_1,c_2,c_4\}$ the ranks of $(c_1,c_2,c_4)$ are $v_1:(1,2,4)$, $v_2:(2,1,3)$, $v_3:(3,2,5)$, $v_4:(5,3,2)$, $v_5:(2,3,1)$. The sum of the two smallest ranks for each voter: $3,3,5,5,3$, total $19$, average $\frac{19}5$. Checking all $\binom53=10$ committees of size $3$, the next best score is $4$ ($\{c_1,c_2,c_3\}$), so $\{c_1,c_2,c_4\}$ is the unique minimizer. ∎

dmm-2022-power-06c.title: Expected sum of the s smallest ranks
dmm-2022-power-06c.body:
For one voter, the ranks of the committee members form a uniformly random $k$-subset $K$ of $\{1,\dots,m\}$, and the voter's contribution is the sum of the $s$ smallest elements of $K$: $\kappa_1+\dots+\kappa_s$ with $\kappa_1<\kappa_2<\dots$. Put $\kappa_0=0$ and $g_i=\kappa_i-\kappa_{i-1}$ for $i=1,\dots,k$, and $g_{k+1}=m+1-\kappa_k$. These $k+1$ gaps sum to $m+1$ and, by the circle argument of 3(c) (choose a random $(k+1)$-subset of $m+1$ points on a circle and a random one of them as origin), all have the same expectation $\frac{m+1}{k+1}$. Hence $\mathbf E[\kappa_i]=\mathbf E[g_1+\dots+g_i]=i\frac{m+1}{k+1}$, and
$$\mathbf E\left[\sum_{i=1}^s\kappa_i\right]=\frac{m+1}{k+1}\sum_{i=1}^si=\frac{s(s+1)}2\cdot\frac{m+1}{k+1}.$$
This holds for every voter, so the average over voters has the same expectation. ∎
